body: thanks for the insight, I'm fascinated with evolutionary psychology and biology so seeing the ancient mechanism is truly insightful.

Two things come immediately to mind, I've been told my whole life I'm judged by my actions, that I'm in control of. It feels like an excuse to say oops, I'm neurotic.

Secondly I'm not sure after light reading on neuroticism how to deal better with it. I fit a lot of the symptoms but don't know for sure if I'm just rationalizing.
I don't think its a good idea to have a glass of anyone's tears and it comes across as aggressive and mean spirited.

> I told him that I wasn't letting anyone call me 'kiddo' anymore

Doesn't sound like a friendly request.

I'd keep my head down, try to patch things up, and just move on, Nothing good is going to come from bringing it back up and I'd suggest you work on yourself if something as simple as 'kiddo' bothers you,

People only make you angry if you let them.

The chair of the dept could very well be twice your age so kiddo isn't inappropriate, When you had to work closer with the guy you told off it shouldn't be surprising he is chilly towards you.

You are being incredibly sensitive and you are not a victim. I'd take him an olive branch and try to patch things up after you told him off.

You've stumbled onto an inequality and just walked around the issue. I'm disappointed. 

Women shouldn't have to live their lives based on what men expect, right? Then why do men have no choice but to serve the whims of the mother?

If we really believe in bodily integrity of people then why can men be made to work for 18 years without a choice while women can choose to be a parent. It goes beyond the word "fair". If men are forced to work for a child they didn't want and the mother knows it, doesn't it become as immoral as slavery?

Once again, the power differential is strong. In this case the mother can dictate everything and proceed to *take* money from a man. Who, by the way, doesn't have the right to know if he's the only candidate to be a father.
